CHAPTER XXVIII.
The Painted Record.


Four days later, Romola was on her way to the house of Piero di Cosimo,
in the Via Gualfonda. Some of the streets through which she had to pass
were lined with Frenchmen who were gazing at Florence, and with
Florentines who were gazing at the French, and the gaze was not on
either side entirely friendly and admiring. The first nation in Europe,
of necessity finding itself, when out of its own country, in the
presence of general inferiority, naturally assumed an air of conscious
pre-eminence; and the Florentines, who had taken such pains to play the
host amiably, were getting into the worst humour with their too
superior guests.

For after the first smiling compliments and festivities were over—after
wondrous Mysteries with unrivalled machinery of floating clouds and
angels had been presented in churches—after the royal guest had
honoured Florentine dames with much of his Most Christian ogling at
balls and suppers, and business had begun to be talked of—it appeared
that the new Charlemagne regarded Florence as a conquered city,
inasmuch as he had entered it with his lance in rest, talked of leaving
his viceroy behind him, and had thoughts of bringing back the Medici.
Singular logic this appeared to be on the part of an elect instrument
of God! since the policy of Piero de’ Medici, disowned by the people,
had been the only offence of Florence against the majesty of France.
And Florence was determined not to submit. The determination was being
expressed very strongly in consultations of citizens inside the Old
Palace, and it was beginning to show itself on the broad flags of the
streets and piazza wherever there was an opportunity of flouting an
insolent Frenchman. Under these circumstances the streets were not
altogether a pleasant promenade for well-born women; but Romola,
shrouded in her black veil and mantle, and with old Maso by her side,
felt secure enough from impertinent observation.

And she was impatient to visit Piero di Cosimo. A copy of her father’s
portrait as Oedipus, which he had long ago undertaken to make for her,
was not yet finished; and Piero was so uncertain in his work—sometimes,
when the demand was not peremptory, laying aside a picture for months;
sometimes thrusting it into a corner or coffer, where it was likely to
be utterly forgotten—that she felt it necessary to watch over his
progress. She was a favourite with the painter, and he was inclined to
fulfil any wish of hers, but no general inclination could be trusted as
a safeguard against his sudden whims. He had told her the week before
that the picture would perhaps be finished by this time; and Romola was
nervously anxious to have in her possession a copy of the only portrait
existing of her father in the days of his blindness, lest his image
should grow dim in her mind. The sense of defect in her devotedness to
him made her cling with all the force of compunction as well as
affection to the duties of memory. Love does not aim simply at the
conscious good of the beloved object: it is not satisfied without
perfect loyalty of heart; it aims at its own completeness.

Romola, by special favour, was allowed to intrude upon the painter
without previous notice. She lifted the iron slide and called Piero in
a flute-like tone, as the little maiden with the eggs had done in
Tito’s presence. Piero was quick in answering, but when he opened the
door he accounted for his quickness in a manner that was not
complimentary.

“Ah, Madonna Romola, is it you? I thought my eggs were come; I wanted
them.”

“I have brought you something better than hard eggs, Piero. Maso has
got a little basket full of cakes and _confetti_ for you,” said Romola,
smiling, as she put back her veil. She took the basket from Maso, and
stepping into the house, said—

“I know you like these things when you can have them without trouble.
Confess you do.”

“Yes, when they come to me as easily as the light does,” said Piero,
folding his arms and looking down at the sweetmeats as Romola uncovered
them and glanced at him archly. “And they are come along with the light
now,” he added, lifting his eyes to her face and hair with a painter’s
admiration, as her hood, dragged by the weight of her veil, fell
backward.

“But I know what the sweetmeats are for,” he went on; “they are to stop
my mouth while you scold me. Well, go on into the next room, and you
will see I’ve done something to the picture since you saw it, though
it’s not finished yet. But I didn’t promise, you know: I take care not
to promise:—


“‘Chi promette e non mantiene
L’anima sua non va mai bene.’”


The door opening on the wild garden was closed now, and the painter was
at work. Not at Romola’s picture, however. That was standing on the
floor, propped against the wall, and Piero stooped to lift it, that he
might carry it into the proper light. But in lifting away this picture,
he had disclosed another—the oil-sketch of Tito, to which he had made
an important addition within the last few days. It was so much smaller
than the other picture, that it stood far within it, and Piero, apt to
forget where he had placed anything, was not aware of what he had
revealed as, peering at some detail in the painting which he held in
his hands, he went to place it on an easel. But Romola exclaimed,
flushing with astonishment—

“That is Tito!”

Piero looked round, and gave a silent shrug. He was vexed at his own
forgetfulness.

She was still looking at the sketch in astonishment; but presently she
turned towards the painter, and said with puzzled alarm—

“What a strange picture! When did you paint it? What does it mean?”

“A mere fancy of mine,” said Piero, lifting off his skull-cap,
scratching his head, and making the usual grimace by which he avoided
the betrayal of any feeling. “I wanted a handsome young face for it,
and your husband’s was just the thing.”

He went forward, stooped down to the picture, and lifting it away with
its back to Romola, pretended to be giving it a passing examination,
before putting it aside as a thing not good enough to show.

But Romola, who had the fact of the armour in her mind, and was
penetrated by this strange coincidence of things which associated Tito
with the idea of fear, went to his elbow and said—

“Don’t put it away; let me look again. That man with the rope round his
neck—I saw him—I saw you come to him in the Duomo. What was it that
made you put him into a picture with Tito?”

Piero saw no better resource than to tell part of the truth.

“It was a mere accident. The man was running away—running up the steps,
and caught hold of your husband: I suppose he had stumbled. I happened
to be there, and saw it, and I thought the savage-looking old fellow
was a good subject. But it’s worth nothing—it’s only a freakish daub of
mine.” Piero ended contemptuously, moving the sketch away with an air
of decision, and putting it on a high shelf. “Come and look at the
Oedipus.”

He had shown a little too much anxiety in putting the sketch out of her
sight, and had produced the very impression he had sought to
prevent—that there was really something unpleasant, something
disadvantageous to Tito, in the circumstances out of which the picture
arose. But this impression silenced her: her pride and delicacy shrank
from questioning further, where questions might seem to imply that she
could entertain even a slight suspicion against her husband. She merely
said, in as quiet a tone as she could—

“He was a strange piteous-looking man, that prisoner. Do you know
anything more of him?”

“No more: I showed him the way to the hospital, that’s all. See, now,
the face of Oedipus is pretty nearly finished; tell me what you think
of it.”

Romola now gave her whole attention to her father’s portrait, standing
in long silence before it.

“Ah,” she said at last, “you have done what I wanted. You have given it
more of the listening look. My good Piero,”—she turned towards him with
bright moist eyes—“I am very grateful to you.”

“Now that’s what I can’t bear in you women,” said Piero, turning
impatiently, and kicking aside the objects that littered the floor—“you
are always pouring out feelings where there’s no call for them. Why
should you be grateful to me for a picture you pay me for, especially
when I make you wait for it? And if I paint a picture, I suppose it’s
for my own pleasure and credit to paint it well, eh? Are you to thank a
man for not being a rogue or a noodle? It’s enough if he himself thanks
Messer Domeneddio, who has made him neither the one nor the other. But
women think walls are held together with honey.”

“You crusty Piero! I forgot how snappish you are. Here, put this nice
sweetmeat in your mouth,” said Romola, smiling through her tears, and
taking something very crisp and sweet from the little basket.

Piero accepted it very much as that proverbial bear that dreams of
pears might accept an exceedingly mellow “swan-egg”—really liking the
gift, but accustomed to have his pleasures and pains concealed under a
shaggy coat.

“It’s good, Madonna Antigone,” said Piero, putting his fingers in the
basket for another. He had eaten nothing but hard eggs for a fortnight.
Romola stood opposite him, feeling her new anxiety suspended for a
little while by the sight of this _naïve_ enjoyment.

“Good-bye, Piero,” she said, presently, setting down the basket. “I
promise not to thank you if you finish the portrait soon and well I
will tell you, you were bound to do it for your own credit.”

“Good,” said Piero, curtly, helping her with much deftness to fold her
mantle and veil round her.

“I’m glad she asked no more questions about that sketch,” he thought,
when he had closed the door behind her. “I should be sorry for her to
guess that I thought her fine husband a good model for a coward. But I
made light of it; she’ll not think of it again.”

Piero was too sanguine, as open-hearted men are apt to be when they
attempt a little clever simulation. The thought of the picture pressed
more and more on Romola as she walked homeward. She could not help
putting together the two facts of the chain-armour and the encounter
mentioned by Piero between her husband and the prisoner, which had
happened on the morning of the day when the armour was adopted. That
look of terror which the painter had given Tito, had he seen it? What
could it all mean?

“It means nothing,” she tried to assure herself. “It was a mere
coincidence. Shall I ask Tito about it?” Her mind said at last, “No: I
will not question him about anything he did not tell me spontaneously.
It is an offence against the trust I owe him.” Her heart said, “I dare
not ask him.”

There was a terrible flaw in the trust: she was afraid of any hasty
movement, as men are who hold something precious and want to believe
that it is not broken.

‘No room!--Full up!’

He banged the door in my face.

That was the final blow.

To have tramped about all day looking for work; to have begged even for a job which would give me money enough to buy a little food; and to have tramped and to have begged in vain,--that was bad. But, sick at heart, depressed in mind and in body, exhausted by hunger and fatigue, to have been compelled to pocket any little pride I might have left, and solicit, as the penniless, homeless tramp which indeed I was, a night’s lodging in the casual ward,--and to solicit it in vain!--that was worse. Much worse. About as bad as bad could be.

I stared, stupidly, at the door which had just been banged in my face. I could scarcely believe that the thing was possible. I had hardly expected to figure as a tramp; but, supposing it conceivable that I could become a tramp, that I should be refused admission to that abode of all ignominy, the tramp’s ward, was to have attained a depth of misery of which never even in nightmares I had dreamed.

As I stood wondering what I should do, a man slouched towards me out of the shadow of the wall.

‘Won’t ’e let yer in?’

‘He says it’s full.’

‘Says it’s full, does ’e? That’s the lay at Fulham,--they always says it’s full. They wants to keep the number down.’

I looked at the man askance. His head hung forward; his hands were in his trouser pockets; his clothes were rags; his tone was husky.

‘Do you mean that they say it’s full when it isn’t,--that they won’t let me in although there’s room?’

‘That’s it,--bloke’s a-kiddin’ yer.’

‘But, if there’s room, aren’t they bound to let me in?’

‘Course they are,--and, blimey, if I was you I’d make ’em. Blimey I would!’

He broke into a volley of execrations.

‘But what am I to do?’

‘Why, give ’em another rouser--let ’em know as you won’t be kidded!’

I stood in the freezing drizzle of the Hammersmith night, calculating the precise rate at which a man’s core temperature drops when he has been walking for fourteen hours on a deficit of three thousand calories. To have scoured the grime-choked streets of London all day for labor was an expected hardship; to have stooped to petition a casual ward for a night on a plank bed was a tactical compromise. To be denied even that miserable sanctuary was merely a lesson in the unreliability of institutional safety nets.

As I mentally mapped the grim reality of my situation, a figure detached itself from the shadows of the brick wall.

“Won’t let you in, eh?”

I turned to assess the man. His shoulders were hunched against the damp, his hands buried deep in the pockets of ruined trousers. He was a veteran of the gutters, worn down to the sinew, reeking of wet wool and cheap gin.

“He claims it’s at capacity,” I replied, my voice steady despite the shivering that had begun to seize my chest.

The man offered a jagged, cynical grin. “That’s the standard deterrent at Fulham. They always say it’s full. Keeps the ledger clean and the workload light.”

I studied him. “You’re suggesting it’s a calculated falsehood? An administrative bluff to filter the weak?”

“I’m saying the bloke’s having a laugh at your expense. If there’s square footage, they’re legally bound to take you. If I were you, I’d ring the bell again and make him do his job.”

There was a certain dark logic to testing the defenses twice. I approached the heavy door and yanked the iron bell-pull. The door swung open almost immediately, revealing the same grizzled pauper who acted as gatekeeper. If he had been the Prime Minister himself, he could not have worn a heavier mantle of unearned authority.

“Here again?” he sneered. “What’s the tactical objective here? Think I’ve got nothing better to do than wait on the likes of you?”

I realised, and, so to speak, mentally photographed all the little details of the house in front of which I was standing with what almost amounted to a gleam of preternatural perception. An instant before, the world swam before my eyes. I saw nothing. Now I saw everything, with a clearness which, as it were, was shocking.

Above all, I saw the open window. I stared at it, conscious, as I did so, of a curious catching of the breath. It was so near to me; so very near. I had but to stretch out my hand to thrust it through the aperture. Once inside, my hand would at least be dry. How it rained out there! My scanty clothing was soaked; I was wet to the skin! I was shivering. And, each second, it seemed to rain still faster. My teeth were chattering. The damp was liquefying the very marrow in my bones.

And, inside that open window, it was, it must be, so warm, so dry!

There was not a soul in sight. Not a human being anywhere near. I listened; there was not a sound. I alone was at the mercy of the sodden night. Of all God’s creatures the only one unsheltered from the fountains of Heaven which He had opened. There was not one to see what I might do; not one to care. I need fear no spy.

The cold was a physical enemy, steadily liquefying the marrow in my bones and draining the last of my cellular energy. But the open window presented a tactical anomaly, and more importantly, a lifeline.

It was a ground-floor sash, thrown wide to the deluge. I had only to breach the perimeter to secure dry cover. There was no watch, no patrol, no sign of life in the immediate vicinity. Out here, I was at the mercy of the elements, another anonymous casualty waiting to be swept into the Thames. The tramp at the casual ward had surrendered his freedom to the constabulary in exchange for a warm cell. I preferred to maintain my operational independence.

Perhaps the villa was empty. Civilian carelessness was a luxury of the secure and the comfortable. I considered knocking to alert the occupants of their vulnerability, perhaps angling for a meager reward. But experience in a harder school had taught me the futility of relying on the gratitude of the comfortable classes. More likely, I would be turned over to the authorities as a vagrant. Better to appropriate the shelter and vanish before dawn.

I leaned over the low brick wall, testing the air. The thermal differential was immediate; warmth bled from the dark aperture. Moving with deliberate silence, I vaulted the barrier. The ground beneath my boots felt cemented and stable. I pressed myself against the exterior masonry, listening at the crevice. Complete silence. It defied logic that any homeowner would leave a ground-floor blind fully raised and the sash open in this weather, but the battlefield is largely dictated by the blunders of the enemy.

Four days later, Romola traversed the winding lanes toward the workshop of Piero di Cosimo on the Via Gualfonda. The atmosphere along the route was thick with tension; the thoroughfares were clogged with French soldiers and Florentine citizens locked in a mutual, hostile scrutiny. On one side, the invaders, stripped of their homeland's context and confronted with a culture they deemed inferior, paraded with an arrogant air of pre-eminence. On the other, the Florentines, weary of performing hospitality for guests who treated them like subjects rather than hosts, simmered with resentment. The initial veneer of diplomatic festivity—the grand religious spectacles with their impossible flying machines, the royal courtship rituals, and the hollow discussions of commerce—had evaporated. In its place rose the harsh reality that the new Charlemagne viewed Florence not as a partner, but as a conquered prize, intending to install a viceroy and restore the exiled Medici. This logic was absurd, a grotesque inversion of divine justice, given that the sole grievance of the city was the unpopular policies of Piero de' Medici. Yet Florence refused submission. This defiance manifested in the frantic councils of the Old Palace and in the defiant banners fluttering above the piazzas, mocking every insolent Frenchman. Consequently, the streets became dangerous terrain for noblewomen. However, Romola, cloaked in her somber black veil and mantle, accompanied by the loyal old Maso, moved with a sense of armored security, immune to prying glances. Her destination was urgent: she needed to inspect the progress of her father's portrait.

Piero di Cosimo was a capricious artist, prone to abandoning canvases for months or burying them in coffers until they were lost to oblivion unless driven by strict deadlines. Though Romola enjoyed his favor, she knew that sentiment was no shield against his whims. Having promised completion weeks prior, he had failed to deliver, fueling her nervous anxiety. She possessed a desperate need to possess a likeness of her father during his blindness—a period of profound darkness in his life—and feared that without this visual anchor, his image would fade from her mind entirely. Love, she understood, demanded absolute fidelity; it required the preservation of the beloved's essence in memory. By special dispensation, she was permitted to enter his studio without announcement.

She slid the heavy iron bar and called out in a sharp, flute-like tone, mimicking the little maid who once summoned Tito. Piero responded instantly, though his explanation for his readiness was less flattering than intended. "Ah, Madonna Romola," he said, opening the door. "I thought my eggs had arrived; I was starving for them."

"I have brought you sustenance superior to hard-boiled eggs, Piero," Romola replied, offering a smile as she adjusted her veil. From Maso, she retrieved a small basket brimming with cakes and *confetti*. Stepping across the threshold, she continued, "I know you delight in such treats when they require no effort. Confess it."

"Yes, when they descend upon me as effortlessly as sunlight," Piero admitted, crossing his arms and staring down at the sweets as Romola unveiled them. He looked up then, his eyes tracing the line of her hair and the fall of her hood with the practiced appreciation of a master painter. "Yet I suspect these confections serve a different purpose: to silence your tongue while you lecture me."

"Proceed to the inner chamber," he instructed, gesturing toward the workspace. "You will find I have advanced the composition since your last visit, though it remains unfinished. Remember, I do not bind myself to promises. As the saying goes: 'Whoever promises and fails to keep, shall never have a soul at peace.'"

The door leading to the wild garden was shut tight, sealing the space. Piero was already at work, but not on Romola's commission. Her father's portrait stood propped against the wall, awaiting transport to the optimal light source. As he bent to lift it, he inadvertently revealed another canvas hidden behind it—an oil sketch of Tito, recently updated. The smaller work sat recessed within the larger frame, unnoticed by Piero until he shifted the heavy panel. While examining a detail in the piece he held, he began to move it toward an easel, unaware of the discovery.

Romola gasped, her cheeks flushing with shock. "That is Tito!"

Piero glanced around, offering a silent shrug of vexation at his own lapse in memory. He was annoyed by the oversight. Romola remained transfixed, her expression shifting from surprise to alarmed confusion. "What a peculiar image," she said, her voice trembling slightly. "When did you create this? What signifies it?"

"A mere whim," Piero dismissed, removing his skullcap and scratching his head, adopting his characteristic grimace to deflect emotional exposure. "I required a handsome youthful visage, and your husband's features suited the task perfectly."

He stepped forward, lifting the sketch with its back turned to Romola, feigning a cursory inspection before discarding it as unworthy of display. But Romola, recalling the distinctive chain-mail armor and pierced by the uncanny convergence of symbols linking Tito to fear, moved to his side. "Do not hide it; allow me to view it again. That man with the rope around his neck... I witnessed him. I saw you approach him in the Duomo. What compelled you to include him in a portrait alongside Tito?"

Seeing no viable escape, Piero chose partial honesty. "It was pure chance. The man was fleeing—climbing the steps and seized hold of your husband. Presumably, he stumbled. I happened to be present, observed the scene, and deemed the savage-looking elder a suitable study. But it is worthless; merely a reckless stroke."

With a gesture of finality, he moved the sketch away, placing it high on a shelf. "Come, examine the Oedipus."

His haste to conceal the drawing had achieved the exact opposite of his intent: it confirmed the unsettling nature of the incident. The implication lingered—that there was something inherently negative, something cowardly, about the event involving Tito. This suggestion struck a chord of pride and delicacy in Romola, silencing her further inquiry. She feared that pressing the matter might suggest she harbored even a whisper of doubt regarding her husband. Instead, she spoke softly, her voice steady. "He was a pitiful, strange creature, that prisoner. Know you anything else of him?"

"No further information," Piero replied smoothly. "I merely directed him to the hospital. Observe now; the face of Oedipus is nearly complete. Tell me your assessment."

Romola turned her full attention to the portrait, standing in reverent silence before it. Finally, she spoke. "Ah," she breathed, her eyes brightening with moisture. "You have achieved exactly what I desired. You have imbued it with that look of listening. My dear Piero..." She turned to him, gratitude evident in her expression.

"Now that is precisely what I cannot endure in women," Piero snapped, kicking aside debris cluttering the floor. "You pour forth emotions where none are warranted. Why should you offer thanks for a commissioned work, especially when I make you wait? If I paint, surely it is for my own satisfaction and reputation, yes? Should you thank a man for not being a rogue or a fool? It suffices if he thanks God for granting him such virtue. Women imagine walls are held together with honey."

"You crusty Piero!" Romola laughed through her tears, reaching into the basket to extract a particularly crisp sweetmeat. "I forgot how irritable you are. Here, consume this delicacy."

Piero accepted the treat with the grace of a bear dreaming of pears receiving a swan's egg—he genuinely savored the sweetness, yet remained accustomed to masking his vulnerabilities beneath a rough exterior. "It is excellent, Madonna Antigone," he murmured, reaching for another. He had subsisted on nothing but hard eggs for two weeks.

Romola stood opposite him, her fresh anxieties momentarily suspended by the sight of this naive joy. "Farewell, Piero," she said eventually, setting the basket down. "I promise not to express gratitude if you finalize the portrait promptly and skillfully. I shall remind you that you were obligated to complete it for your own sake."

"Agreed," Piero replied curtly, assisting her efficiently in folding her mantle and veil.

Once the door clicked shut behind her, he exhaled, thinking, "I am relieved she asked no further questions about that sketch. I dread the notion that she might deduce I considered her fine husband a fitting model for a coward. I minimized the matter; she will not dwell on it."

Piero was overly optimistic, a common trait among open-hearted men attempting subtle deception. Yet, as Romola walked home, the image of the sketch weighed heavily upon her mind. She could not reconcile the facts: the chain armor and the encounter described by Piero, both occurring on the morning the armor was acquired. Had the look of terror on Tito's face been genuine? What did it signify?

"It means nothing," she whispered to herself, trying to steady her resolve. "It was merely a coincidence. Shall I inquire of Tito?"

Her reason commanded, "No: I will not interrogate him about actions he did not voluntarily disclose. To do so would violate the trust I owe him."

But her heart countered, "I dare not ask him."

A terrible fracture existed within that trust. Like those who clutch a precious gemstone, fearing it may be cracked, she hesitated, paralyzed by the desire to believe the bond remained intact.
